body:
Childhood & Early Life

George Herbert was born on 3 April 1593 at Montgomery Castle on the Welsh border, into one of the great families of the region. His father, Richard, died when George was three, which left his mother Magdalen to raise a house full of children, ten of them, alone. She was no ordinary widow. Magdalen Herbert ran a lively household and a circle of poets, and John Donne was her friend and wrote verse to her. George grew up with a mind that was sharp, ambitious, and constantly being watched by a formidable woman.

He went to Westminster School and then to Trinity College, Cambridge, where he became a Fellow in 1616. His older brother Edward became the courtier-philosopher Lord Herbert of Cherbury. George was expected to climb too.

What He Did & Why He's Remembered

At Cambridge he was made Public Orator in 1620, the university's official voice, which meant writing polished Latin speeches to kings and nobles. It was the job you took if you wanted a career at court. He sat in Parliament in 1624. And then the door closed: King James died in 1625 and so did the friends who might have lifted him. Herbert turned toward the church, was ordained, and at thirty-seven took the small parish of Bemerton near Salisbury, a tiny place nothing like the life he had been chasing.

He is remembered because of what he did there, quietly, in the last three years of his life. He wrote the poems of The Temple, some of the most honest conversations with God in the English language. They are not pious in a polished way. They argue, sulk, rebel, and give in. He also wrote A Priest to the Temple, a practical guide to being a country parson.

Family Life

The shadow of his father's early death and the strength of his mother run through everything. When Magdalen died in 1627, Donne preached her funeral sermon and Herbert wrote Latin poems for her. Later at Bemerton he looked after his nieces, and accounts of his life describe a man who visited the sick, gave to the poor, and played music with neighbours. He and his brother Edward were very different men from one family.

Romantic Life

As far as the record shows, Herbert did not have famous romances. In 1629 he married Jane Danvers, who came from a Wiltshire family that had long hoped for the match. Izaak Walton, his first biographer, tells the story of a quick, almost shy courtship. They had no children, and she outlived him and remarried. The great love story of his work is the one in "Love (III)" below, where the lover is God, and the way it is written, he is the one who cannot accept being loved.

Life Until Death

Herbert had tuberculosis for much of his life and by Bemerton he knew he was dying. He died on 1 March 1633, a few weeks short of forty. On his deathbed he reportedly handed his poems to his friend Nicholas Ferrar of Little Gidding, saying to publish them only if they might help "any dejected poor soul", and otherwise to burn them. Ferrar published The Temple that same year. It was a bestseller and went through many editions.

His Works

These are Herbert's original spellings from The Temple (1633).

The Collar
I struck the board, and cry'd, No more;
I will abroad.
What? shall I ever sigh and pine?
My lines and life are free; free as the rode,
Loose as the winde, as large as store.
Shall I be still in suit?
Have I no harvest but a thorn
To let me bloud, and not restore
What I have lost with cordiall fruit?
Sure there was wine
Before my sighs did drie it: there was corn
Before my tears did drown it.
Is the yeare onely lost to me?
Have I no bayes to crown it?
No flowers, no garlands gay? all blasted?
All wasted?
Not so, my heart: but there is fruit,
And thou hast hands.
Recover all thy sigh-blown age
On double pleasures: leave thy cold dispute
Of what is fit, and not. Forsake thy cage,
Thy rope of sands,
Which pettie thoughts have made, and made to thee
Good cable, to enforce and draw,
And be thy law,
While thou didst wink and wouldst not see.
Away; take heed,
I will abroad.
Call in thy deaths head there: tie up thy fears.
He that forbears
To suit and serve his need,
Deserves his load.
But as I rav'd and grew more fierce and wilde
At every word,
Me thoughts I heard one calling, Childe:
And I reply'd, My Lord.

This is the rebellion poem. The speaker slams the table and says he will leave; then one word undoes it.

Love (III)
Love bade me welcome: yet my soul drew back,
Guiltie of dust and sinne.
But quick-ey'd Love, observing me grow slack
From my first entrance in,
Drew nearer to me, sweetly questioning,
If I lack'd any thing.

A guest, I answer'd, worthy to be here:
Love said, you shall be he.
I the unkinde, ungratefull? Ah my deare,
I cannot look on thee.
Love took my hand, and smiling did reply,
Who made the eyes but I?

Truth Lord, but I have marr'd them: let my shame
Go where it doth deserve.
And know you not, sayes Love, who bore the blame?
My deare, then I will serve.
You must sit down, sayes Love, and taste my meat:
So I did sit and eat.

Often called one of the finest poems in English. It is a welcome, and a man too ashamed to accept it.

Redemption
HAving been tenant long to a rich Lord,
Not thriving, I resolved to be bold,
And make a suit unto him, to afford
A new small-rented lease, and cancell th' old.

In heaven at his manour I him sought:
They told me there, that he was lately gone
About some land, which he had deerly bought
Long since on earth, to take possession.

​

I straight return'd, and knowing his great birth,
Sought him accordingly in great resorts;
In cities, theatres, gardens, parks, and courts:
At length I heard a ragged noise and mirth
Of theeves and murderers: there I him espied,
Who straight, Your suit is granted, said, & died.
The Pulley
When God at first made man,
Having a glasse of blessings standing by;
Let us (said he) poure on him all we can:
Let the worlds riches, which dispersed lie,
Contract into a span.

​

So strength first made a way;
Then beautie flow'd, then wisdome, honour, pleasure:
When almost all was out, God made a stay,
Perceiving that alone of all his treasure
Rest in the bottome lay.

For if I should (said he)
Bestow this jewell also on my creature,
He would adore my gifts in stead of me,
And rest in Nature, not the God of Nature,
So both should losers be.

Yet let him keep the rest,
But keep them with repining restlesnesse:
Let him be rich and wearie, that at least,
If goodnesse leade him not, yet wearinesse
May tosse him to my breast.
Prayer (I)
PRayer the Churches banquet, Angels age,
Gods breath in man returning to his birth,
The soul in paraphrase, heart in pilgrimage,
The Christian plummet sounding heav'n and earth,

Engine against th' Almightie, sinners towre,
Reversed thunder, Christ-side-piercing spear,
The six-daies world-transposing in an houre,
A kinde of tune, which all things heare and fear,

Softnesse, and peace, and joy, and love, and blisse,
Exalted Manna, gladnesse of the best,
Heaven in ordinarie, man well drest,
The milkie way, the bird of Paradise,

Church-bels beyond the starres heard, the souls bloud,
The land of spices; something understood.
The Flower
How fresh, O Lord, how sweet and clean
Are thy returns! ev'n as the flow'rs in spring;
To which, besides their own demean,
The late-past frosts tributes of pleasure bring.
Grief melts away
Like snow in May,
As if there were no such cold thing.

Who would have thought my shrivel'd heart
Could have recover'd greennesse? It was gone
Quite under ground,as flow'rs depart
To see their mother-root, when they have blown;
Where they together
All the hard weather,
Dead to the world, keep house unknown.

These are thy wonders, Lord of power,
Killing and quickning, bringing down to hell
And up to heaven in an houre;
Making a chiming of a passing-bell,
We say amisse,
This or that is:
Thy word is all, if we could spell.

O that I once past changing were,
Fast in thy Paradise, where no flow'r can wither!
Many a spring I shoot up fair,
Offring at heav'n, growing and groning thither:
Nor doth my flower
Want a spring-showre,
My sinnes and I joyning together.

​

But while I grow in a straight line,
Still upwards bent, as if heav'n were mine own,
Thy anger comes, and I decline:
What frost to that? what pole is not the zone,
Where all things burn,
When thou dost turn,
And the least frown of thine is shown?

And now in age I bud again,
After so many deaths I live and write;
I once more smell the dew and rain,
And relish versing: O my onely light,
It cannot be
That I am he
On whom thy tempests fell all night.

These are thy wonders, Lord of love,
To make us see we are but flow'rs that glide:
Which when we once can finde and prove,
Thou hast a garden for us, where to bide.
Who would be more,
Swelling through store,
Forfeit their Paradise by their pride.
epi: The Welsh courtier who gave up ambition and wrote what a restless heart sounds like
